<div class="banner">
<strong>What we found:</strong> At 31 °C, coral fragments became paler, lost algae from their tissue, and gained less skeletal mass. Wounds still sealed, but only 4 of 12 heated fragments budded new corallites, the small skeletal cups on a regrown tip, by Day 15. All 12 fragments at 28 °C did so. Fragments from source patch C were less affected by heat than those from A and D.<br>
<strong>Genetic update:</strong> Final host-genotype groups are now available for the 144 early samples; the Day 15 fragments remain ungenotyped. A, C, and D still name the field source patches. Symbiont read typing remains rough.<br>
<strong>Species name:</strong> Species identification remains provisional: <em>Acropora cf. pulchra</em>. The abbreviation <em>cf.</em> means “compare with” and indicates that the species identification is uncertain. We retain <em>A. pulchra</em> here to match the project’s existing labels.
</div>

We kept coral fragments at <span class="t28">28 °C</span> or <span class="t31">31 °C</span> and clipped the growing tip on half of them. Over 15 days, we measured wound repair, skeletal growth, color, photosynthesis efficiency, and the algae living in coral tissue, called **algal symbionts**.

## The experiment

- 8 tanks: four held at <span class="t28">28 °C</span>, four at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>
- Half the fragments had the growing tip clipped; half were left unwounded
- 3 field source patches: A, C, D. A source patch is where the parent material came from; these patches are not yet confirmed genetic individuals.
- Tissue samples collected on Days 1, 3, 10, and 15
- The 48 fragments sampled on Day 15 were also followed for coral condition and regrowth; 24 were wounded
- A separate experiment followed wound covering in 16 wounded fragments using microscope photos

```{r, fig.cap=cap_design}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide05_experimental_design.png"))
```

We wounded each clipped fragment by removing the growing tip. The Day 0 photo below shows the fresh cut surface.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_wound_day0}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide14_morphology_heated_D0.png"))
```

## What we found

### 1. The +3 °C temperature difference held

All eight tanks have 144 readings per day, one every ten minutes, from Day 0 through Day 15 (4–19 June 2025). Daily tank means averaged **27.78 °C** in the 28 °C treatment and **30.87 °C** in the 31 °C treatment, a **3.09 °C difference**. Each treatment had four tanks.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_apex}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("08_apex_temperature.png"))
```

The temperature record is complete through Day 15. Treatment averages exclude later days, after the main experiment ended.

### 2. Heat reduced coral condition; average growth was also lower

At <span class="t31">31 °C</span>, fragments became paler, gained less skeletal mass, and lost algal symbionts. Their photosynthesis-efficiency score, **Fv/Fm**, also fell. This score measures how efficiently the algae’s photosynthetic system can use light.

These changes occurred in clipped and unwounded fragments. We found little evidence that tip clipping added to the decline caused by heat. This does not establish that clipping has no effect, or that a local wound response is absent.

- Photosynthesis score and color declined through time under heat.
- Symbiont density dropped sharply over the two weeks.
- Skeletal mass gain was **34% lower** at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>. Because temperature was assigned to tanks, the test uses four tanks per treatment as the independent replicates. The growth difference remains uncertain (*p* = 0.057).

**Heat and wounding across three measures of coral condition**

```{r, fig.cap="Candidate Figure 2. Heat and wounding across photosynthesis efficiency (A), algal symbiont density (B), and skeletal growth (C). Columns separate 28 °C (blue) and 31 °C (orange). Open symbols and white boxes indicate unwounded fragments; filled symbols and gray boxes indicate wounded fragments. A follows the same 48 fragments over seven visits. Points average four tank means per temperature and wound state; bars show one standard error among tank means. Tip and base readings are averaged within each fragment first. B compares different fragments sampled on Days 1, 3, 10, and 15, with 12 fragments per temperature-by-wound group on each day (192 total). C shows percent skeletal mass gain over 15 days in 48 fragments, with 12 per group. In B and C, dots are individual fragments; boxes show the median and middle half of values, with whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5 box lengths. Boxes are side by side for comparison, not statistically paired samples or confidence intervals. Temperature inference uses four tanks per treatment, not individual dots as independent replicates. Source patches are combined in this display, not removed from the models. Day 0 marks clipping; Day −1 is not an unheated baseline. Missing values are not filled."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("45_physiology_figure2.png"))
```

The corrected wound assignment is included throughout the physiology analyses. Each temperature now has 12 wounded and 12 unwounded Day 15 fragments. Photosynthesis follows the same fragments over time; symbiont density compares different fragments at each sampling day, so those measurements are shown as separate distributions rather than connected trajectories.

**Near the tip versus near the base.** We measured photosynthesis efficiency about 1 cm from each end of every fragment. All 48 fragments have both readings at all seven visits. Both locations declined under heat, so the overall heat response does not depend on averaging them.

From Day 0 onward, the tip score averaged 0.012 below the base at 28 °C and 0.021 below it at 31 °C. The estimated extra tip-to-base difference under heat was small and uncertain: −0.009 score units (95% interval −0.023 to 0.006; tank-level test, *p* = 0.20). The gap varied through time, but the tank-level comparison did not clearly show different time patterns between temperatures (*p* = 0.143). We also found no clear added effect of clipping on the gap.

The two-location average remains useful for describing overall fragment condition. It does **not** mean the locations are equivalent or that a local response near the wound is absent. We retain both readings for the location comparison.

```{r, fig.cap="Both sampled locations lost photosynthesis efficiency under heat. Upper panels show readings about 1 cm from the tip (green) and base (purple), separately for clipped and unwounded fragments. Thin lines are observed tank means; thick lines average the four tanks per temperature. Lower panels show the paired difference, near-tip minus near-base, calculated within each fragment before averaging by tank. Negative values mean lower efficiency near the tip. Each tank contributes two to four fragments per recorded wound state. Day −1 is before clipping, not an unheated baseline; statistical comparisons use Days 0–14. Lines describe observations, not model fits or uncertainty bands."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("42_pam_location_comparison.png"))
```

```{r, fig.cap="Heated fragments became paler. Panels separate temperatures and lines distinguish wounded and unwounded fragments (yes/no). Lower color scores mean paler tissue; the axis is reversed, so lower scores appear higher on this plot. Points are observed means across fragments and shaded bands show one standard error on either side, not tank-adjusted confidence intervals. Day 0 marks clipping. Source patches are combined."}

### 3. Wounds re-covered, but fewer heated fragments budded new corallites

Wounds re-covered with living tissue quickly at both temperatures. Only **4 of 12 heated fragments (33%)** had budded new corallites, the small skeletal cups on the rebuilt tip, by Day 15. All **12 of 12 fragments at 28 °C (100%)** had done so. A longer experiment might have allowed more heated fragments to reach this step; these data cannot tell us whether the delay was permanent.

Here, **healing** means the coenosarc, the sheet of living tissue between coral polyps, re-covered the wound. **Regeneration** means the later rebuilding steps: the main polyp forms, the wound surface remodels, the tip returns, the tip extends, and new corallites bud.

The healing panel uses a separate microscope-photo experiment with 16 wounded fragments, eight per temperature. The other panels use the 24 wounded fragments in the main experiment, 12 per temperature. All 16 microscope fragments were recorded as covered on Day 1. The microscope photos illustrate the stages in a separate group; they cannot verify individual scores in the main experiment.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_stage_cumulative}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("39b_stage_timing_cumulative_option.png"))
```

The curves show the percentage first recorded at each stage by each day. Each percentage includes all fragments, including those that had not reached the stage. Once a fragment has a positive score, it remains counted, even if a later score marks the feature absent. A later absence may reflect a real change or a scoring inconsistency; these curves do not distinguish the two.

```{r}
stage_summary_tbl <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path("..", "..", "output", "tables", "36_molly_stage_timing_mean_iqr.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stage_names <- c("Living tissue covers wound", "Main polyp forms",
                 "Wound surface remodels", "Tip forms", "Tip extends",
                 "New skeletal cups bud")
attainment <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(Stage = stage_names[stage_order],
                value = sprintf("%d/%d (%.0f%%)", n_reached, n_scored, pct_reached)) |>
  dplyr::select(Stage, treatment, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = value)
knitr::kable(attainment, caption = paste(
  "Fragments observed at each stage at least once by Day 15.",
  "Tissue cover uses the separate microscope-photo experiment; other rows use the main experiment."
))
```

This differs from asking whether a feature was **present on Day 15 itself**. The table and curves show whether each fragment had reached a stage at least once by that day. They do not assume that every stage follows a fixed order or that a feature remains visible afterward.

**Average time to each stage.** Each point averages the first observation days of fragments that reached that stage. Filled points include every fragment; open points leave out those that had not reached the stage by Day 15. The counts show how many contribute. We keep the percentage-by-day plot above as the main comparison because it includes all fragments.

```{r, fig.cap="Average first-observation days among fragments that reached each stage. Blue = 28 °C; orange = 31 °C. Points show means; horizontal lines show the middle half of observed first days, not confidence intervals. Open points average only fragments that reached the stage by Day 15. Right-hand labels give reached/total counts. Tissue cover uses 8 fragments per temperature from the separate microscope experiment; other stages use 12 per temperature from the main experiment. In particular, the final heated-stage mean describes only 4 of 12 fragments and cannot represent the full heated group."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("40_stage_mean_review.png"))
```

For incomplete stages, these averages favor the fragments that finished sooner. They do not estimate when the others would finish. The table below therefore keeps averages only for stages reached by every fragment at both temperatures.

```{r}
complete_timing <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(complete_both_temperatures) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Stage = stage_names[stage_order], Temperature = treatment,
                   `Mean first-observation day` = mean_day,
                   `Middle half of first days` = iqr_days)
knitr::kable(complete_timing, digits = 2, caption = paste(
  "Timing summaries for stages reached by all fragments at both temperatures.",
  "The middle-half range runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile.",
  "These are first observation days, not exact biological onset times.",
  "All 16 microscope fragments had tissue cover recorded on Day 1."
))
```

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_violin}

<details>
<summary>Exact observation days for each fragment</summary>

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_timing}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("36_molly_stage_timing.png"))
```

</details>


**What the scores tell us.** The reviewed records show tip formation in 11 of 12 fragments at each temperature, rather than all 12. Budding can occur in the wound area before visible tip extension, so these stages are not a strict sequence. The budding result remains 12/12 at 28 °C versus 4/12 at 31 °C.

Pigment was assessed on Days 3, 4, 9, 12, and 15 in the main experiment. Other days remain unknown, not absent. Pigment is not one of the six stages above, and its sparse observations support a less precise timing comparison.

**How the timing models handle unfinished stages.** A fragment that had not reached a stage by its final observation contributes “not yet reached” information. It is not dropped or assigned an invented completion day. For fragments that did reach a stage, the main timing model places onset between the last absent score and the first present score.

The existing model estimates a **1.32-fold longer time** to new-corallite budding at 31 °C. This is a model estimate, not the average time of the four heated fragments that budded. It assumes a particular pattern of event times and adjusts for source patch; its uncertainty does not account for fragments sharing a tank. The observed 4/12 versus 12/12 result does not depend on that model.

A closed wound is not the same thing as a regenerated tip. If we scored only wound sealing, we would miss the main heat effect.

The two fragments shown below both seal the wound and rebuild a tip. Only the fragment at 28 °C buds new corallites by Day 15.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_timeline}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide15_morphology_timeline.jpg"))
```

The time-lapse follows these two fragments from Day 0 to Day 15: 28 °C on the left and 31 °C on the right.

   <source src="data:video/mp4;base64,%s" type="video/mp4"></video>

  xfun::base64_encode(img(f)), cap)
cat(vid("morphology_ambient_healing.mp4",
        "28 °C time-lapse: the wound seals, the tip rebuilds, and new corallites bud by Day 15."),

```

### 4. Source patch C was hurt less by heat

Fragments from **source patch C** retained more of their photosynthesis efficiency, color, and algal symbionts under heat than fragments from A and D. Growth followed the same pattern, but the evidence for a growth difference is weaker.

We compare each patch at 31 °C with the same patch at 28 °C. That tells us how much heat changed its response, rather than which patch had the highest starting value.

The condition measurements consistently point to smaller heat effects in C. The size of the difference depends on the response and its measurement scale; there is no single fold difference that describes C's heat tolerance.

The figures below summarize these differences as a **heat penalty**: how much worse a response was at 31 °C than at 28 °C. Each measurement is put on a relative scale before the penalties are averaged.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_source_summary}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19e_source_heat_penalty_summary.png"))
```

In the summary plot, source patch C stays near zero overall. Source patches A and D have bigger estimated condition, growth, and regrowth penalties. The early-repair category describes features in the main experiment, not direct wound-cover measurements; those came from the separate microscope cohort. Timing-based scores are exploratory.

The four condition and growth measurements each show a smaller estimated heat penalty for C.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_source_physiology}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19f_source_physiology_heat_penalties.png"))
```

The next plot shows the measurements used in the combined score.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_genet_dashboard}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19_genet_dashboard.png"))
```

The final plot focuses on wound repair and regrowth.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_wound_heat}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19d_wound_healing_heat_penalties.png"))
```

**How the heat-penalty score is built**

The score has two steps.

**Step 1: calculate the heat effect for each source patch within each measurement.**

For whole-fragment condition and growth:

\[
\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement} =
\text{estimated value at }28^\circ\text{C} - \text{estimated value at }31^\circ\text{C}
\]

For these measurements, higher values mean better coral condition or growth. A positive heat effect means the source patch did worse at 31 °C.

The symbiont-density model uses the natural logarithm of cell density. Its heat effect is therefore a difference in log density, equivalent to the logarithm of the 28 °C-to-31 °C density ratio, not a difference in cell counts. Photosynthesis score, color, and percent growth use their own measurement scales before scaling in Step 2.

For repair timing, the model compares how quickly fragments reach a step while they have yet to reach it. This comparison is called a **hazard ratio (HR)**: the rate at 31 °C divided by the rate at 28 °C.

\[
\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement} =
-\log(\text{HR}_{31^\circ\text{C} / 28^\circ\text{C}})
\]

If HR is below 1, the step occurred more slowly at 31 °C. Taking its natural logarithm and reversing the sign gives a positive heat penalty.

**Step 2: put each measurement on the same scale, then average.**

\[
\text{scaled heat penalty}_{source,measurement} =
\frac{\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement}}
{\max(|\text{heat effect}_{A,measurement}|,\ |\text{heat effect}_{C,measurement}|,\ |\text{heat effect}_{D,measurement}|)}
\]

This makes the largest source-patch difference within each measurement equal to 1 in size. It keeps the sign: positive means worse or slower at 31 °C; negative means better or faster at 31 °C.

\[
\text{source heat-penalty score}_{source} =
\text{mean of scaled heat penalties across usable measurements}
\]

We compare temperatures within each measurement before combining the effects. Photosynthesis score and color use Day 14, symbionts use the final tissue sample, and growth uses the full 15-day change. Those comparisons average wounded and unwounded fragments. Repair timing uses wounded fragments only.

The combined scores are **C = `r source_score("c")`, A = `r source_score("a")`, and D = `r source_score("d")`**. Each averages ten effects. They summarize relative responses, not a formal test of differences among patches. Sparse pigment observations and unstable timing estimates limit this combined score; the separate condition measurements provide the clearer evidence for C's smaller heat response.

**Possible trade-offs**

A trade-off would mean that better performance in one response comes with worse performance in another. Source patch C grew less at 28 °C but lost less growth under heat. The pattern remains when growth is left out of the heat-penalty score. Still, this comparison has only three source patches. A plot of growth against growth lost under heat also uses the 28 °C growth value on both axes, so it cannot establish a trade-off on its own.

We found **no clear growth cost of regeneration** in the 12 heated wounded fragments. Fragments that budded new corallites gained 0.57 percentage points more mass, on average, than those that did not. That difference was uncertain (*p* = 0.196).

After accounting for source patch, the estimated growth difference was `r sprintf("%.2f", tradeoff_adjusted$estimate)` percentage points (95% interval `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", tradeoff_adjusted$lower_ci, tradeoff_adjusted$upper_ci)`; *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", tradeoff_adjusted$p_value)`). The raw and adjusted comparisons therefore do not support a growth cost. Growth and regrowth were measured over the same period, so neither comparison identifies cause and effect.

Models that followed when each fragment reached a stage also found no clear evidence that faster growth went with slower repair. Checks that reduced the influence of unusual observations, or omitted one fragment at a time, did not change that conclusion.

Some growth estimates were sensitive to individual fragments. With only 12 heated wounded fragments, we cannot rule out a smaller cost. These results show no clear trade-off so far; they do not show that regeneration is cost-free.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_tradeoff_summary}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("35_tradeoff_summary.png"))
```

### 5. Final DNA-marker groups and the algae they host

The final DNA-marker results group fragments by genetic similarity. The markers are **single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)**, differences at individual DNA positions. They came from **RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)**, which measures gene activity and can also reveal some DNA differences.

A group of genetically similar samples is called a **cluster**. The final set has eight host-genotype clusters. All 144 fragments retain their earlier cluster assignments; the final genetic-coordinate values replace the preliminary values. These assignments apply to the sequenced fragments, not automatically to other fragments collected from the same source patch.

The file matches 144 tissue samples prepared for sequencing, called **libraries**, using each fragment’s identifying number:

- All **48 samples from C** fall in cluster 1.
- The 48 samples from A fall in clusters 4, 5, 6, and 7, mostly cluster 4.
- The 48 samples from D fall in clusters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8.
- A and D share clusters 4 and 5.

```{r, fig.cap="Final host-genotype clusters preserve the earlier group memberships. Left: each point is one of 144 sequenced fragments, positioned using the first two summaries of DNA-marker differences from the final SNP set. Colors identify field source patches. Right: counts in each genetic cluster, split by source patch; labels identify the larger segments. Cluster sizes are 48, 17, 16, 52, 7, 2, 1, and 1. Host clusters and source patches are different groupings."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_structure.png"))
```

All sequenced fragments from source patch C belong to host cluster 1. A and D each contain several clusters and share clusters 4 and 5. We assigned treatments by source patch before these genetic results were available. Final assignments do not fix the resulting imbalance: some clusters have few samples or no samples in particular treatment combinations.

```{r, fig.cap="Final clusters are unevenly represented across treatments. Each tile gives the number of sequenced fragments for a host cluster, temperature, sampling day, and clipping treatment. Zero means an empty combination, not a missing genetic assignment. Clusters 7 and 8 have only heated samples; cluster 6 has one fragment per temperature. These groups cannot support a well-replicated comparison of heat responses."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_design.png"))
```

**Which responses can we link to DNA markers?** The current 144 sequenced fragments were sampled on Days 1, 3, and 10. Symbiont density is the only response measured on those same fragments that we can directly link to these markers.

The 48 fragments sampled on Day 15 have the broader response record: photosynthesis score and color through Day 14, growth and symbiont density at Day 15, and regrowth through Day 15. We do not yet have DNA-marker results for those fragments.

The current plan is to move ahead with the existing samples rather than delay the paper for new sequencing. The final host assignments can inform expression analyses where treatment combinations overlap. They do not add Day 15 genetic assignments or gene-expression measurements.

```{r, fig.cap="Measured symbiont density within final host clusters. Each point is one fragment; color distinguishes temperature and shape distinguishes clipping. Sampling days remain separate rather than being pooled into a genetic effect. The vertical scale shows millions of algal cells per square centimeter, with equal spacing for equal fold changes. Small horizontal offsets separate overlapping points. These are observations, not adjusted treatment estimates, and fragments in a tank are not independent temperature replicates."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_density.png"))
```

The updated density analysis accounts for tank, sampling day, clipping, and host cluster. It retains a smaller estimated heat-related loss in cluster 1 than in clusters 2–4. This pattern remains when we leave out fragments dominated by other symbiont groups. It is a reanalysis of the same density data, not independent confirmation of genetic control. Small, uneven groups and imperfect model fit keep these comparisons exploratory; clusters 6–8 are shown but not included in the fitted cluster comparisons.

**Which algae dominate?** The new file also compares sequence reads with four reference symbiont genomes. A read is a short piece of sequence; the relative share mapping to each reference provides a rough picture of the symbiont mixture. Group A, identified as *Symbiodinium*, dominates **138 of 144 fragments**. Five are dominated by group D and one by C. These symbiont letters are unrelated to our coral source-patch letters or host-cluster numbers.

```{r, fig.cap="Rough symbiont typing from sequence-read mapping. Each bar is a fragment; colored portions show the reported relative shares for reference groups A, B, C, and D, which sum to one. Panels are final host clusters, with sample counts shown; bar widths therefore differ among panels. Fragments are ordered by their group-A share, not by time. These shares are not measured cell proportions or symbiont density, and a dominant group does not imply that no other group is present."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_typing.png"))
```

All six non-A-dominated fragments were heated and clipped; five were sampled on Day 10 and one on Day 1. We cannot tell from these data whether heat changed their symbiont mixture or whether they differed beforehand. This makes the mixture worth checking in expression analyses, but it is not evidence that symbiont type caused the heat response. Host assignments are final; this symbiont typing remains rough, and updated expression results are still pending.

**How the Hauru colonies might connect.** A preliminary survey of Hauru colonies by Trinity Conn and Ross Cunning provides a possible link to short-term heat responses. It lists colony locations, genetic groups, the most common symbionts, and responses to a short heat test.

Their heat-response measure is **ED50**: the temperature at which the photosynthesis-efficiency score falls halfway during that test. It describes a short exposure, not how long a coral can tolerate weeks of heat.

Source patch C is **10.5 m from Apul-115**, whose ED50 is 36.380 °C. A and D are closest to Apul-111. Nearby colonies can be genetically identical across field patches, so distance alone cannot identify a match.

Trinity’s table places Apul-115 in clonal group 2, a group of colonies identified as genetically identical, and labels its dominant symbiont “A.” That symbiont label is unrelated to our source patch A. These details may help guide a comparison of our DNA markers with the Hauru whole-genome data.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_trinity_hauru_context, out.extra='class="hauru-map"'}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("26b_trinity_hauru_context.png"))
```

Apul-115 and Apul-111 are candidates for genetic comparison. Their ED50 values cannot yet be assigned to source patches A, C, or D.

### 6. Weeks of heat affected corals below their short-test heat limit

Our <span class="t31">31 °C</span> treatment was **4.4 °C below** the mean short-test ED50 of 35.4 °C reported by Cunning et al. (2024). ED50 is the temperature at which the photosynthesis-efficiency score falls halfway during a short heat test.

That comparison puts the treatment in context. It does not make 35.4 °C a safe limit for a longer exposure or establish the limit of our particular fragments.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_thermal_context}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("26_thermal_context.png"))
```

Even at 31 °C, sustained exposure reduced coral condition and the percentage that budded new corallites by Day 15. This was the last recorded stage, not a test of complete functional recovery.

## Take-homes

- **The temperature difference held.** All eight tanks have a complete logger record through Day 15, with a mean difference of 3.09 °C.
- **Heat reduced coral condition.** Heated fragments had lower photosynthesis scores, paler color, fewer symbionts, and lower average skeletal growth. The growth difference is less certain. We found little evidence of added harm from tip clipping; that is not proof of no wound effect.
- **Wound covering and later regrowth differed.** Wounds re-covered quickly at both temperatures. Only 4/12 heated wounded fragments budded new corallites by Day 15, compared with 12/12 at 28 °C. We do not know whether the others would have budded later.
- **Source patch C was less affected by heat.** The clearest differences were in photosynthesis score, color, and symbiont density. Its 48 sequenced fragments all belong to final host cluster 1; the Day 15 fragments remain ungenotyped.
- **Trade-offs remain unresolved.** C grew less at 28 °C but lost less growth under heat. Within heated wounded fragments, we found no clear evidence that regrowth came at a cost to growth. The small sample cannot rule out a cost.
- **Final host groups are available, but the genetic question remains limited by the design.** The 144 assignments are unchanged from the preliminary set. Only symbiont density directly overlaps these fragments. Most have group-A-dominated symbiont reads; the six exceptions all occur in heated, clipped fragments, so host and symbiont explanations need care.

## Open questions

- **How does genetic identity affect the expression comparison?** Use the final assignments where treatment groups overlap. Linking identity to the broader Day 15 phenotype record would still require new genotyping; that is not a prerequisite for the current paper.
- **Which gene responses accompany slower regrowth?** Gene-expression comparisons can test whether heat changes activity associated with rebuilding the wounded tip.
- **Do short-test heat responses predict performance during sustained heat?** Confirmed DNA matches to the Hauru colonies would allow this comparison.
- **How certain are the repair-timing estimates?** The corrected scores are incorporated. Timing uncertainty still needs to account for fragments sharing a tank, and pigment timing is limited by gaps between observations.

## How much confidence to place in the results

The observed wound-cover and budding counts do not depend on a fitted timing model. Heat effects on coral condition are supported by repeated-measurement analyses and checks of alternative time patterns. Temperature was assigned to tanks, so the four tanks per treatment, not the individual fragments, are the independent temperature replicates.

Some daily yes/no morphology models have unstable estimates because nearly every fragment shares the same score at some stages. We do not use their very small reported *p*-values as evidence. Repair-timing models still need fuller tank-level uncertainty checks. The combined heat-penalty score, three-patch trade-off comparisons, and uneven genetic-cluster comparisons remain exploratory. A model fitting successfully does not resolve these limitations.
